name: Kira Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for meeting me, Kira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no links to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a curtain-sider for Brennan Freight, a regional haulier with about forty trucks. A curtain-sider is a trailer with fabric sides you pull back, so a forklift can load from the side. Most days I do eight to ten drops to builders' merchants, tile shops and garden centres across three counties, and I'm home most nights. I like being trusted to run my own day, and I hate waiting two hours at a shop that booked the wrong delivery slot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been driving, and what's life like at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years, four at Brennan's. I'm married to Imran, he's a self-employed plumber, and we rent a terrace near the industrial estate. We've got about four months saved, and the long-term plan is for me to buy my own truck and work for myself. I use AI every day, for finding return loads, checking my hours, doing our accounts, all of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it did what I expected: helped with the boring bits and stopped there. At the depot I'd tell the lads it's still worth using, because it saves me an hour of paperwork a week. Online I'd probably post a little guide to the apps I use for loads and hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means my plan carries on. I want my own truck by thirty, running as an owner-driver with contracts from a couple of builders' merchants I already know. A world where nothing changes is a fine world to start a small business in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for Brennan's and save hard for the deposit on a used tractor unit, maybe fifteen thousand. I'd do the operator's licence course next year, the one you need to run your own trucks, which is a few hundred pounds and some exams. And I'd keep using AI for quotes and accounts, so I'm ready when I go it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited about my own plans, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Imran think about you going self-employed too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's all for it, he's done it for five years. His advice is always the same: find two good customers before you buy anything. He'd want me to have the contracts lined up first, and he's right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any worry in this picture at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Diesel prices and interest rates, mostly. If the bank wants silly money for a truck loan, the whole plan waits. That's a bigger worry for me than any computer.

I'd tell drivers it's still worth it, saving me **an hour** of paperwork weekly.
think: I think it means **my plan carries on**: my own truck by thirty.
A world where nothing changes is a **fine world** to start a small business.
do: Save towards a **£15,000 deposit** on a used tractor unit.
Take the **operator's licence** course next year.
Keep using AI for **quotes and accounts** to prepare.
feel: She feels **calm** and **excited** about her own plans.

fieldNote: She's a **would-be owner-driver** with a clear target: her own truck by thirty.
Her worries are **diesel and loan rates**, not technology.
Husband Imran's **self-employed experience** shapes her cautious, contracts-first approach.

steps.text: Save towards a £15,000 deposit on a used tractor unit
Take the operator's licence course next year
Line up two builders' merchants as future customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good time for drivers who use the tools and a hard time for those who won't. At Brennan's, the planning office would be first to feel it, and I'd say so. Online I'd say small operators can now do what only big firms could afford.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's good for me. If AI does quotes, bookings and invoices, a one-truck business doesn't need an office. That's exactly the bit that puts most drivers off going self-employed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring my plan forward a year and buy the truck at twenty-nine. I'd use an AI booking system for my own loads and let it chase invoices. I'd also keep an eye on the freight exchange, because if big firms cut planners, they'll need owner-drivers to pick up extra loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a bit of a buzz. I'd also feel bad for the office people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which office people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our planners at Brennan's, mainly. There's four of them, and two are older ladies who've been there twenty years. I don't think the firm would keep them all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd bring the plan forward. What if robots then come for your truck?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this picture they come slowly, so I'd have years of driving. If robots come for the trucks, I'd want to be the one who owns the truck, not the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and anyone in trucking who isn't planning is kidding themselves. I'd post about it, and I'd tell the lads at Brennan's to start saving. I'd also say the government shouldn't stop it, but it should make sure ordinary people can own a piece of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. Two years to AGI, five to robot trucks, and I'm thirty-two with a loan on a truck that's suddenly worth nothing. My whole plan was built on a human driver being needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shelve buying a diesel truck straight away, because it would lose value fast. I'd keep driving for Brennan's and save everything, and look at getting into the driverless side as a dispatcher or a small fleet owner. If I could, I'd go in with Imran's cousin, who has some money, to buy one autonomous truck when they're available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be thinking fast, but my stomach would be in knots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Imran's work fare in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than mine, I think. Plumbing in old houses is fiddly, so robots would take longer. That's some comfort, because one of us would be earning while I figured it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ordinary people should own a piece. What would that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Small operators should be able to buy and run driverless trucks, not just big companies. If the giants own them all, people like me are finished. I'd want the chance to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and a smart driver uses it. I'd tell other drivers at the depot to learn the new systems and think about owning, not just driving. Online I'd keep posting what I learned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's tight but workable. Eight years until robot trucks means I can buy a diesel truck at twenty-nine, run it for five years and pay it off before the robots arrive. Then I'd sell it and switch to running autonomous trucks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the used truck in two years, work it hard, and pay off the loan fast. I'd learn fleet management software and keep up with the autonomous truck trials. I'd also save some money in shares in logistics or AI firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more in control. I'd feel the clock ticking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the plan fall apart?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robot trucks came early or the bank wouldn't lend. Or if prices for used trucks crashed before I paid mine off. I'd watch those three things like a hawk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Imran change any family plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on kids until the truck was paid off. Imran's mum would grumble, she wants grandchildren. But I'd rather have a stable base first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and we'd be fools to waste it. Drivers should treat it like an apprenticeship for the new world. Online I'd share how I planned to get there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be excited. Ten years to build a business, own trucks, learn the systems and be ready when robots arrive. I'd be thirty-nine by then, with my own small firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy my first truck at twenty-nine, run it, then add a second one with a hired driver by thirty-two. I'd learn every bit of the autonomous systems as they come. By the late 2030s I'd want to switch to driverless trucks and run a small fleet from a laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. More eager than worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the drivers you might hire and later replace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That bothers me, honestly. I'd tell them straight from the start, and I'd help them train for something else. I wouldn't string anyone along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And your faith or family, how does that fit this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd have kids by the early 2030s, God willing. Imran would keep plumbing, I'd run the business. Family first, but the business keeps the family.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd be stuck with a diesel truck nobody wants and no time to change course. What would help is fair access for small firms to buy driverless trucks, and banks willing to lend to owner-drivers who want to switch.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the robots. Everyone talks about losing jobs, but the real question is who gets the profit when the robots drive the trucks. If drivers can own the trucks, this could be the best thing that ever happened to us.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about losing jobs, but the real question is who gets the profit when the robots drive the trucks.
portrait: Kira is a **27-year-old multi-drop driver** at Brennan Freight, married to Imran, a self-employed plumber.
She **uses AI daily** and plans to become an owner-driver by thirty.
In the mild scenarios she sees AI as **removing the office barrier** to self-employment.
In the fast AGI picture she fears a **worthless truck loan** and pivots to owning driverless trucks.
With ten years she's **eager**, planning a small fleet run from a laptop.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she'd be stuck with a diesel truck nobody wants.
whatWouldHelp: Fair access for **small firms** to driverless trucks, and banks willing to lend to **owner-drivers**.
